title: Socially Responsible AI Algorithms: Issues, Purposes, and Challenges
abstract: In the current era, people and society have grown increasingly reliant on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. AI has the potential to drive us towards a future in which all of humanity flourishes. It also comes with substantial risks for oppression and calamity. Discussions about whether we should (re)trust AI have repeatedly emerged in recent years and in many quarters, including industry, academia, healthcare, services, and so on. Technologists and AI researchers have a responsibility to develop trustworthy AI systems. They have responded with great effort to design more responsible AI algorithms. However, existing technical solutions are narrow in scope and have been primarily directed towards algorithms for scoring or classification tasks, with an emphasis on fairness and unwanted bias. To build long-lasting trust between AI and human beings, we argue that the key is to think beyond algorithmic fairness and connect major aspects of AI that potentially cause AI’s indifferent behavior. In this survey, we provide a systematic framework of Socially Responsible AI Algorithms that aims to examine the subjects of AI indifference and the need for socially responsible AI algorithms, define the objectives, and introduce the means by which we may achieve these objectives. We further discuss how to leverage this framework to improve societal well-being through protection, information, and prevention/mitigation. This article appears in the special track on AI & Society.

claims.text: Existing technical solutions for AI responsibility are narrow in scope, focusing primarily on scoring or classification tasks with an emphasis on fairness and unwanted bias.
A survey by Doteveryone revealed that 59% of tech workers have worked on products they felt were harmful to society.
A survey by Doteveryone revealed that more than 25% of AI workers who experienced working on harmful products quit their jobs as a result.
An investigation into Princeton Review online tutoring prices showed that Asian customers were 1.8 times more likely to be charged higher prices regardless of income.
Social Responsibility of AI can be structured into a four-level hierarchy consisting of functional, legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities.
Socially Responsible AI Algorithms operationalize societal well-being across three functional dimensions: protecting users, informing users, and preventing or mitigating negative impacts.

limitations.text: Prior research in responsible AI is narrowly focused on independent topics like fairness or interpretability in scoring/classification tasks, lacking a holistic view of sociotechnical relations.
Model transparency introduces security paradoxes where disclosures and post-hoc explanations can be purposefully manipulated or exploited by adversaries.

future_work.text: Incorporating causal learning methods to address model robustness, transferability, and cause-effect explanations in responsible AI.
Designing context-aware socially responsible AI algorithms that integrate social context and algorithmic feedback loops.
Developing provably robust AI defenses ('AI firewalls') that automatically detect weak spots and intercept malicious inputs.
Modeling temporal dynamics and feedback loops to evaluate and guarantee long-term algorithmic fairness.
